what: OpenText sells information management software. Its products store, organise, secure and route an organisation’s documents, records and data — content management, business process automation, cybersecurity, backup and analytics — assembled over two decades by buying dozens of software companies.
customers: Large organisations and governments worldwide that need to manage documents and data under regulatory requirements, plus small business customers of its acquired security and backup products.
money: Recurring cloud and subscription revenue across the product portfolio.
Maintenance on licensed software, highly recurring and highly profitable.
New perpetual licences and professional services.
moat: OpenText’s model is to buy mature software that customers depend on and cannot easily replace, then run it efficiently and collect the maintenance revenue. Document and records management systems hold years of an organisation’s files under regulatory retention rules, which makes migration genuinely difficult — so the revenue persists even when the product is not growing.
risks: Debt of $6.0B against $956.0M of cash is very heavy, a legacy of the acquisition strategy, and it exceeds the market value.
Revenue fell from $5.8B in 2024 to $5.2B after a large acquisition was partly divested, and the underlying business grows slowly at best.
The strategy depends on finding more software to buy at sensible prices, and the balance sheet currently limits that.
Many of the products are mature or declining, and customers migrating to modern cloud alternatives do eventually leave.
Eleven analysts average a $28.14 target, about 26% above the current price.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $844.8M against a $5.4B market value is a 16% yield, and the shares trade at about 6.4 times free cash flow.
The shares trade at about 8.5 times earnings and 6.4 times EV/EBITDA.
Maintenance revenue on installed software is among the most predictable revenue in any industry.
Document and records management holds data under regulatory retention rules, which makes migration slow and expensive for customers.
A net margin of about 12.5% on $5.2B of revenue shows the acquired portfolio is run efficiently.
watch: Organic revenue growth and the cloud subscription line. The maintenance revenue is reliable but slowly shrinking, and whether cloud growth offsets it is what determines the company’s direction.
view: OpenText does something unglamorous and economically sound: it buys mature enterprise software that customers cannot easily stop using, runs it with tight cost discipline, and collects the maintenance revenue. The products are frequently not the best available and often not growing. That is not the point. The point is that an organisation with fifteen years of regulated documents in a records management system does not migrate casually, and keeps paying maintenance year after year.

The economics of that are genuinely attractive. Free cash flow of $845 million against a $5.4 billion market value is a 16% yield, at 6.4 times free cash flow and 8.5 times earnings. Maintenance revenue on installed enterprise software is among the most predictable revenue streams in any industry, and the net margin of about 12.5% shows the portfolio is being run efficiently rather than merely harvested.

The thing that determines whether this works is the debt, and it is substantial: $6.0 billion against $956 million of cash, which exceeds the market value. The acquisition model requires borrowing to buy, then using the acquired cash flow to repay. That is fine while the cash flow is stable and refinancing is available, and it is the source of real fragility if either changes. Revenue falling from $5.8 billion to $5.2 billion after a partial divestment is the strategy in reverse.

So the question is whether this is a well-run consolidator temporarily constrained by its balance sheet, or a collection of declining software being levered and harvested. The honest answer is that it is somewhat both, and the ratio matters more than the label. The maintenance base is reliable and slowly shrinking; cloud subscription growth is what has to offset it. Organic revenue growth and the cloud line are the two disclosures that tell you which direction the business is actually moving, and at a 16% free cash flow yield you are being paid well to find out.
bull: Cloud subscriptions offset slowly shrinking maintenance revenue while debt reduction transfers value to equity, and a 16% free cash flow yield compounds.
bear: Mature products decline faster than cloud grows, $6.0 billion of debt exceeding the market value refinances at higher rates, and the consolidation engine cannot restart.
